cards.claim: Law of conservation of mass (Lavoisier): in all physical and chemical changes there is no net change in mass; matter can neither be created nor destroyed.
cards.quote: in all physical and chemical changes, there is no net change in mass duting the process. Hence, he reached to the conclusion that matter can neither be created nor destroyed. This is called ‘Law of Conservation of Mass’.

cards.claim: Law of definite proportions (Proust): a given compound always contains exactly the same proportion of elements by weight.
cards.quote: He stated that a given compound always contains exactly the same proportion of elements by weight.

cards.claim: Law of multiple proportions (Dalton): when two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in a ratio of small whole numbers.
cards.quote: According to this law, if two elements can combine to form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other element, are in the ratio of small whole numbers.

cards.claim: Avogadro's law: equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.
cards.quote: Avogadro proposed that equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure should contain equal number of molecules.

cards.claim: Gay Lussac's law of gaseous volumes (gases combine or form in simple volume ratios) holds only when all the gases are at the same temperature and pressure.
cards.quote: are produced in a chemical reaction they do so in a simple ratio by volume, provided all gases are at the same temperature and pressure.

locator.section: 1.5.4 Gay Lussac's law of gaseous volumes

cards.claim: Dalton's atomic theory explains the laws of chemical combination but not the law of gaseous volumes, nor why atoms combine.
cards.quote: Dalton’s theory could explain the laws of chemical combination. However, it could not explain the laws of gaseous volumes. It could not provide the reason for combining of atoms

cards.claim: NCERT multiple-proportions example: in water and hydrogen peroxide, the masses of oxygen (16 g and 32 g) that combine with a fixed 2 g of hydrogen are in the simple ratio 16:32, or 1:2.
cards.quote: Here, the masses of oxygen (i.e., 16 g and 32 g), which combine with a fixed mass of hydrogen (2g) bear a simple ratio, i.e., 16:32 or 1: 2.

cards.claim: Hydrogen and oxygen gases consist of diatomic molecules; Avogadro explained the combining volumes by treating the molecules as polyatomic.
cards.quote: In fact, Avogadro could explain the above result by considering the molecules to be polyatomic. If hydrogen and oxygen were considered as diatomic as recognised now, then the above results are easily understandable.
